sections.label: Learning goals
sections.final_normalized_text: Learning goals1. Outcome Overview & Core ConceptsTitles use capital letters. Which additional words take capitals depends on the chosen style; names keep their capitals. Commas separate items in a list so the reader can see each item clearly.Big idea: Use capital letters in titles and commas to separate listed itemsLearning routine: Identify title or list → Apply punctuation → Read aloud → Edit

sections.label: Subject-Specific Content & Key Examples
sections.final_normalized_text: Subject-Specific Content & Key Examples2. Subject-Specific Content & Key ExamplesEdit a title and a listTheSecretGardenapples, pears and grapesThe title uses capitals; the list uses commas between items.Use punctuation to guide readingMy Trip to the Reefpencils, rulers, glue and papercapital letterscommasRead the sentence aloud and listen for the small pauses between list items.Sort and noticeEdit a set of book titles and shopping lists.Guided practiceSort and notice — Edit a set of book titles and shopping lists.Build or improve — Create a title and a four-item list, then swap for peer editing.Explain your choice — Use the words title, capital letter, comma to explain what you changed and why.Actual title and list editing cardsFor this activity, use title case: capitalise the first word and main words; keep internal a, an, the, and, or, to and of lower-case unless part of a proper name. Title cards: “the red kite”; “a walk to the pond”; “mia and the moon”. Models: “The Red Kite”, “A Walk to the Pond”, “Mia and the Moon”. Another valid style is sentence case: “A walk to the pond”. Apply the declared style for the task. List draft: “We packed a red hat two blue pens a ruler and paper.” Whole items: a red hat / two blue pens / a ruler / paper. Edit: “We packed a red hat, two blue pens, a ruler and paper.” A clear serial comma before and is also accepted unless a stated style excludes it. Do not split red from hat or blue from pens. End the sentence with its full stop.
